chunks.title: Trauma assessment & chemical injury
chunks.tldr: Life first (ABC), then history: blunt vs sharp, high vs low velocity (hammering metal on metal → IOFB), prior eye surgery, last meal. Inspect without pressing on the globe; pupils (RAPD), VA with pinhole/near card, fields; then ophthalmology for slitlamp, IOP, fundus. Chemical burn = irrigate immediately (tap water on scene, saline in ED) with anaesthetic + speculum, remove particles (cement/plaster), continue until neutral pH. Alkali (bleach, cement, lime, cleaners) penetrates (saponification) — worse than acid (car battery; protein precipitate barrier). Severe signs: corneal haze, limbal blanching (ischaemia), chemosis — a white eye can be the worst. Then: antibiotic, cycloplegic, steroid, ascorbate (topical + oral), citrate, oral doxycycline (anti-MMP), lubricants, acetazolamide for IOP.
chunks.hook: A white eye after alkali = limbal ischaemia, not mild.

cards.q: Why does doxycycline help after chemical burns?
cards.a: It inhibits matrix metalloproteinases (collagenase), reducing corneal melting, and is anti-inflammatory.

cards.q: End point of irrigation in a chemical injury?
cards.a: Neutral pH (≈7) of the tear film, checked a few minutes after stopping.

chunks.title: Open globe injury & IOFB
chunks.tldr: Full-thickness corneal/scleral defect: laceration (sharp/projectile; penetrating = entry only, perforating = entry + exit; ± retained object) or rupture (blunt; weak points — behind muscle insertions (superonasal), old surgical wounds, limbus, lamina). Signs: peaked pupil toward wound, flat AC, uveal prolapse, 360° haemorrhagic chemosis, very soft eye, hyphaema/VH, deep lid laceration; Seidel positive. Do: rigid shield (no patch/pressure), analgesia, antiemetic, NBM, tetanus, systemic antibiotics, CT for IOFB (no MRI if metal). Theatre ASAP under GA without succinylcholine; 10-0 nylon cornea, 8-0/9-0 sclera; reposit viable uvea; lens/posterior IOFB usually second stage (vitreoretinal). Iron/copper/organic IOFB → remove (siderosis, chalcosis, endophthalmitis).
chunks.hook: Suspected open globe: Shield, Scan, Starve, Surgery — never press.

cards.q: Why avoid succinylcholine when repairing an open globe?
cards.a: It transiently raises IOP (extraocular muscle contraction), risking extrusion of intraocular contents.

cards.q: Most common site of blunt globe rupture?
cards.a: Behind the rectus muscle insertions (thinnest sclera), especially superonasally, or at previous surgical wounds.

chunks.title: Abrasion, foreign body, SCH, lacerations & traumatic iritis
chunks.tldr: Corneal abrasion: fingernail, CL; pain relieved by anaesthetic drop; fluorescein stains; topical antibiotic ± patch; review. Never send home with anaesthetic drops (delay healing, neurotrophic ulcer). Foreign body: grinding/hammering; remove at slitlamp with 25–27 G needle; rust ring → burr; vertical linear abrasions → evert upper lid (subtarsal FB). Consider penetration — Seidel, dilate. Subconjunctival haemorrhage: >270° or with chemosis → suspect occult rupture. Partial-thickness lacerations: confirm depth at slitlamp. Traumatic iritis: 24–48 h later, photophobia, cells/flare, Vossius ring; cycloplegic + steroid (ophthalmologist).
chunks.hook: Linear vertical scratches on the cornea = something under the top lid.

cards.q: Why must patients not be given topical anaesthetic to take home?
cards.a: It inhibits epithelial healing, masks worsening, and causes toxic/neurotrophic keratopathy with prolonged use.

chunks.title: Hyphaema & angle injuries
chunks.tldr: Hyphaema: torn iris/ciliary vessels; layered blood (grade by height) or microhyphaema; may signal open globe. Risks: raised IOP, rebleed (days 3–5), corneal blood staining (high IOP + big bleed → amblyopia in kids), sickle cell (sickling in AC → high IOP, optic nerve vulnerable; avoid CAIs). Rx: bed rest head up, shield, topical steroid + cycloplegic, IOP drops, ± oral aminocaproic acid; AC washout for uncontrolled IOP/staining. Concussive damage: sphincter tears, iridodialysis (root disinsertion, D-shaped pupil), cyclodialysis (ciliary body off spur → hypotony), angle recession (torn ciliary face → late glaucoma; gonioscopy/UBM), lens sub/luxation (phacodonesis).
chunks.hook: Black kid + hyphaema → sickle test before acetazolamide.

cards.q: Complication of hyphaema that threatens amblyopia in young children?

cards.a: Cyclodialysis cleft (aqueous drains to the suprachoroidal space).

chunks.title: Posterior segment & optic nerve trauma
chunks.tldr: Commotio retinae (Berlin oedema): retinal whitening opposite impact within 24 h, fades over days–weeks; macula → VA loss; no treatment. Choroidal rupture: crescent concentric to disc, through Bruch's/RPE; macular → poor VA; late CNV (treatable). Traumatic macular hole: vitrectomy possible, VA often poor. Traumatic VH: usually with PVD; clears unless retinal tear → RD (B-scan). Traumatic optic neuropathy: frontal blow (indirect, optic canal), apex fracture, penetrating, gouging; RAPD; steroids controversial (CRASH), decompression unproven.
chunks.hook: Crescent scar around the disc after a blow = choroidal rupture → watch for CNV.

cards.q: Orientation of a traumatic choroidal rupture?
cards.a: Crescent-shaped, concentric to the optic disc (usually temporal).

chunks.title: Lid lacerations, blowout fractures & retrobulbar haemorrhage
chunks.tldr: Lid lacerations: check margin, canaliculi (medial), canthi, and the globe beneath; margin/canalicular injury → ophthalmic/oculoplastic repair (align tarsus, grey line, lashes; stent canaliculus). Blowout fracture (floor > medial wall): enophthalmos/exophthalmos, infraorbital numbness (V2), diplopia (upgaze), crepitus, rim step. White-eyed blowout in children: trapdoor IR entrapment with minimal external signs, pain, oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea) → urgent repair. Others: repair in 1–2 wk if persistent diplopia or enophthalmos (>2 mm, large fracture). CT orbits (neuroradiology), look for facial/skull fractures. Retrobulbar haemorrhage (orbital compartment syndrome): tense proptosis, ↓VA, RAPD, high IOP, ↓motility → immediate lateral canthotomy + inferior cantholysis. Orbital FB: organic → remove (infection, MRI shows wood); metal often left; lead inert, copper inflammatory.
chunks.hook: Tight orbit + RAPD = cut the canthus now, scan later.

cards.q: Why is a 'white-eyed blowout' an emergency in children?
cards.a: Trapdoor entrapment of the inferior rectus causes muscle ischaemia and oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, vomiting) despite a quiet-looking eye.

chunks.title: Burns, UV keratitis & late sequelae
chunks.tldr: Thermal lid burns: lubricate/antibiotic ointment; full-thickness → cicatricial ectropion/retraction in days → tarsorrhaphy, grafts. UV keratitis (welding arc, snow, tanning beds): pain hours later, punctate staining — treat like abrasion. Late: irregular astigmatism (RGP, graft after 6 mo), LSCD (limbal transplant then KP/keratoprosthesis), hypotony (<6 mmHg — leak, cyclodialysis, RD, occult rupture, inflammation → phthisis), endophthalmitis (contaminated/organic, retained FB — Bacillus), corneal blood staining, siderosis (iron: heterochromia, rust, mydriasis, ERG decline) / chalcosis (copper: KF ring, sunflower cataract), sympathetic ophthalmia (enucleate a blind ruined eye within ~10 days), monocular (corneal) vs binocular (nerve/muscle/fracture) diplopia, epiphora from canalicular/NLD injury (DCR/Jones tube). Team with maxillofacial, plastics, neurosurgery.
chunks.hook: Iron makes the eye go brown-green and the ERG go flat — remove it.

cards.a: Iris heterochromia (darker), rust-coloured anterior subcapsular deposits, mydriasis, pigmentary retinopathy with progressive ERG reduction.
